claims.text: Nanoparticles containing five or more metals in near-equal atomic ratios maintain structural and chemical stability from 473 to 1923 K.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the disordered solid-solution phase.
Configurational-entropy stabilization counteracts enthalpic forces that drive phase segregation.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions.
High configurational entropy lowers the free energy of mixing at temperatures within the catalytic and thermoelectric operating range.
Lowering the free energy of mixing suppresses atomic segregation.
Temperature-activated atomic diffusion can cause phase separation if it exceeds the stabilizing effect attributed to configurational entropy.
Under the stated conditions, the nanoparticles will show minimal phase segregation throughout 473–1923 K.
Under the stated conditions, the nanoparticles will retain a uniform, single-phase structure throughout 473–1923 K.
Phase composition and morphology will change negligibly relative to the as-synthesized room-temperature state.
The temperature at which diffusion overcomes entropic stabilization depends on the particular metal combination and particle size.
The predicted stability is conditional on an inert atmosphere, minimal contamination or oxidation, and a heating protocol that avoids melting or excessive diffusion.

contradictions.description: The prediction asserts stability across the entire 473–1923 K range, while the boundary and uncertainty fields allow diffusion to exceed entropic stabilization at an unspecified, system-dependent temperature that could lie within that range.
